title: Travel Influencer Left With Over 100 Bed Bug Bites After One Night at Budget Hotel
excerpt: Hannah Stephenson's viral TikTok documenting bleeding welts from a Travelodge stay in Cambridge, England, reignites scrutiny of bed bug prevention in the hospitality industry.
body:
• UK content creator Hannah Stephenson, 31, woke up covered in more than 100 bed bug bites after a single night at a Travelodge hotel in Cambridge, England, with bites spreading across her arms, legs, chest, and face.
  • Stephenson said she felt "ignored" by Travelodge until her TikTok post documenting the ordeal went viral with over 100,000 views, after which the hotel chain offered £2,000 (approximately $2,700) in compensation.
  • The incident highlights a broader resurgence of bed bug problems in the hospitality sector, with recent cases including a $50,000 lawsuit against a Walt Disney World resort in Florida.

A UK travel influencer is warning fellow travelers after a one-night stay at a budget hotel left her covered in more than 100 bleeding bed bug bites that have persisted for weeks, sparking a viral social media backlash against the hospitality chain.

Hannah Stephenson, 31, checked into the Travelodge on Newmarket Road in Cambridge, England, after an evening out with friends rather than making the long drive home. She woke to itching, blood spots on her pillow, and the bugs themselves crawling on the bed.

More Than 100 Bites in One Night

The bites covered Stephenson's arms, legs, chest, and face. She counted more than 37 on one hand alone. Three weeks later, the welts have not fully healed, spreading further and causing swelling in her arms and visible marks on her face.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites. It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realized what had happened."

— Hannah Stephenson

"I've had to take a lot of antihistamines, which have made me quite drowsy. I've been waking up in the night itching," Stephenson told the BBC. "I have felt very self-conscious. There are certain social events I haven't gone to, as I was so embarrassed at the way my arms were looking and the way my face looked."

The experience forced her to buy new clothing to cover the bites for a family wedding. She has lived in Asia, Africa, and South America without encountering bed bugs, making the Cambridge incident all the more unexpected.

Viral Post Forces Hotel Response

Stephenson initially felt "ignored" when she reported the problem to Travelodge. It was only after she posted graphic photos and videos of her bites on TikTok — garnering more than 100,000 views — that the hotel chain engaged with her directly. Commenters urged her to pursue legal action, writing "This is a NIGHTMARE!!" and "You absolutely need to SUE for this."

Stephenson has since accepted £2,000 (approximately $2,700) in compensation from Travelodge but said she hopes the company improves its prevention standards.

A Travelodge spokesperson told the BBC: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and recognise how distressing an incident like this can be. The safety of our customers is our priority, and we maintain stringent, expert-led measures to prevent and manage pest issues."

The company said that when an issue is reported, affected and surrounding rooms are immediately taken out of service for inspection and treatment by independent pest control experts. Travelodge also noted that bed bug activity "affects the wider hospitality sector and is completely unrelated to hygiene or cleanliness standards."

A Growing Problem for Travelers

The incident is part of a broader resurgence of bed bug problems across the global hospitality industry. In the United States, a Walt Disney World visitor recently filed a $50,000 lawsuit alleging he was bitten multiple times during a stay at the All-Star Sports Resort in Florida. Los Angeles was recently ranked the second-worst US city for bed bugs, behind Chicago.

According to the British Pest Control Association, bed bugs are not a reflection of cleanliness standards — they are brought into environments through luggage, clothing, and personal belongings. Medical researchers warn that beyond the physical discomfort, bed bug infestations can cause secondary skin infections, chronic sleep deprivation, and psychological distress that is "frequent but underestimated."

How Travelers Can Protect Themselves

Travel experts recommend inspecting hotel mattress seams, headboards, and furniture joints before settling into any room. Keeping luggage on hard surfaces rather than the floor or bed, and checking for small rust-colored stains on sheets, can help catch infestations early. If bites are discovered, documenting the evidence with photos and reporting immediately to both the hotel and local health authorities strengthens any subsequent complaint or claim.
